messages.content: Maintain a 2:1 ratio of declarative to interrogative sentences in your response. Show a metric space (M, d) is complete if and only if any sequence (F_n) of nonempty closed subsets of M with - F_{n+1} \subset F_n - diam F_n \rightarrow 0 as n \rightarrow \infty has a nonempty intersection

message.content:
The theorem states that a metric space is complete if and only if every nested sequence of nonempty closed sets with vanishing diameter has a nonempty intersection. This equivalence provides a fundamental characterization of completeness in topological spaces.

Is the forward direction intuitive? Yes, because any convergent subsequence must converge to a point within the closed limit set. Does this imply that Cauchy sequences converge? Indeed, since the diameters shrink to zero, the distance between any two terms eventually becomes arbitrarily small. Is the converse also true? If the intersection is empty, we can construct a Cauchy sequence that does not converge, proving the space is incomplete.
